title: Indian Diamond Trader Dhiru Ramani Freed in Mali After Family Pays €4 Million Ransom
excerpt: The 75-year-old Surat businessman and two other Indian hostages were released after nearly three months in captivity; his family says it negotiated with the Al-Qaeda-linked group without government help.
body:
• Dhiru Ramani, a 75-year-old diamond businessman from Surat with operations in New York, was freed in Mali after his family paid a ransom of €4 million (roughly ₹44 crore).
  • Two other Indian nationals — his cook and an electrician — were also released after nearly three months in captivity by a group believed to be linked to Al-Qaeda affiliate JNIM.
  • The kidnappers initially demanded €10 million; the family says it negotiated the release independently without assistance from the Indian government.
  • The incident has triggered concern among Surat-based industrialists with mining and business operations across Africa.

Dhiru Ramani, a 75-year-old Gujarati diamond trader with businesses spanning Surat, New York and West Africa, was freed in Mali this week after his family reportedly paid a ransom of approximately €4 million to an armed group suspected of ties to Al-Qaeda.

Two other Indian nationals — Ramani's cook and an electrician — were released alongside him. All three were brought to Bamako, Mali's capital, where Ramani underwent preliminary medical checks and was found to be in stable condition, according to a family member who spoke to the Times of India.

Three Months in Captivity

The kidnapping took place roughly three months ago, though the precise date and location have not been publicly disclosed. Ramani had been in Mali for the past two years, overseeing a gold mining venture he entered after stepping back from the diamond trade.

The abductors did not contact the family for nearly two months after seizing the three men. When ransom demands finally came, the group — believed by family sources to be linked to Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), Al-Qaeda's largest affiliate in the Sahel — asked for €10 million, equivalent to roughly ₹100 crore.

"The family has no option but to negotiate with the abductors to secure the safe release of the three Indians. The family's priority is to bring them back safely."

— A close relative of Dhiru Ramani, speaking on condition of anonymity

Negotiations intensified over the final 10 days. The family, based in the United States, verified Ramani's condition through a video call arranged by the captors before agreeing to pay roughly 40 percent of the original demand.

Family Says Government Was Not Involved

In an unusual disclosure, family members told Indian media that the entire negotiation was handled without any involvement from the Indian Ministry of External Affairs or other government agencies. The family communicated directly with the armed group from the United States.

India's embassy in Bamako has not publicly commented on the release. The MEA had previously issued advisories urging Indian nationals in Mali to "exercise utmost caution" following a string of kidnappings in the country.

A Growing Pattern in the Sahel

Ramani's abduction fits a broader trend. JNIM has made kidnapping wealthy foreigners a core revenue strategy in what analysts call "economic jihad." According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), at least 22 foreign nationals were abducted in the Sahel between May and October 2025 alone — nearly double the record set in 2022. Victims have included Chinese, Indian, Emirati, Iranian and Egyptian citizens.

The most high-profile case involved a member of Dubai's ruling family, kidnapped in September 2025, for whom the UAE reportedly paid more than $20 million. That deal also included the release of dozens of imprisoned JNIM militants.

In July 2025, three Indian nationals working at a cement factory in Kayes, western Mali, were abducted by armed assailants. Five more Indians were kidnapped in a separate incident later that year. Mali's military government, which took power in a 2021 coup, has struggled to contain JNIM despite assistance from Russian mercenaries.

Diaspora Business Community on Edge

Ramani's release has brought relief to Surat's diamond and jewellery industry, where his family is well known. He owns Ramani Export in New York City and CBD Diamond & Jewellery showrooms. His sons are US citizens active in the international diamond trade.

But the incident has also rattled industrialists with investments in African mining and manufacturing. Several Surat-based businessmen with overseas operations are closely watching the case, according to Dainik Bhaskar.

Ramani is expected to travel to the United States to rejoin his family. Originally from Dhar village in Amreli district, Gujarat, he had shifted from natural diamonds into lab-grown diamonds and jewellery before diversifying into gold mining in Mali roughly two years ago.

What's Next

Indian authorities face mounting pressure to address the safety of citizens working in conflict zones across the Sahel. With eight Indians kidnapped in Mali in 2025 alone and the security situation showing no signs of improvement, the MEA's travel advisories may need to be backed by more concrete protective measures for the estimated 400 Indians still living in the country.
